title: The Crab Nebula, Hubble Space Telescope mosaic
creator: NASA, ESA and J. Hester (Arizona State University), Hubble Space Telescope
why_public_domain: A NASA Hubble Space Telescope image. NASA material is not copyrighted in the US, and OpenStax credits it to NASA/ESA. The ESA co-credit is the one soft spot (see report).
original_holder: NASA/ESA Hubble; reproduced in OpenStax Astronomy 2e, chapter 1 opener
caption: The wreck of the star that Chinese and Japanese astronomers recorded as a "guest star" in July 1054. It was bright enough to see in daylight for about three weeks. Its tangled gas is still spreading outward today, about 6,500 light-years away.

title: Lord Rosse's six-foot telescope at Birr Castle
creator: Unknown engraver (book illustration)
why_public_domain: A wood engraving in Robert Ball's 1897 book. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Robert S. Ball, The Story of the Heavens (new ed., London: Cassell, 1897), Fig. 7, via Project Gutenberg #27378
caption: The giant reflector the third Earl of Rosse built in Ireland. Rosse made his 1844 sketch of the nebula with a smaller three-foot telescope, which is where the name "Crab" comes from. He observed it again later with this six-foot instrument.

title: The comet panel of the Bayeux Tapestry (colour facsimile)
creator: Unknown embroiderers (England, c. 1070s); colour facsimile in Belloc's book
date: Event April 1066; tapestry c. 1070s; facsimile published 1914
why_public_domain: A faithful reproduction of an eleventh-century textile, printed in 1914. The tapestry is out of copyright everywhere, and an exact copy of it creates no new copyright.
original_holder: Hilaire Belloc, The Book of the Bayeux Tapestry (London: Chatto & Windus, 1914), panel 35, via Project Gutenberg #60727
caption: Men point up at the comet under the words ISTI MIRANT STELLA ("these men wonder at the star"). Next to them, a courtier bends to warn the newly crowned King Harold. Below them sit empty ghost ships, a hint of the invasion to come.

title: The Comet (Bayeux Tapestry, photographic plate)
creator: Unknown embroiderers (c. 1070s); photograph reproduced by the Victoria and Albert Museum
why_public_domain: A straight photograph of an eleventh-century textile, printed in a 1914 museum guide. It is out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Victoria and Albert Museum, A Guide to the Bayeux Tapestry (London, 1914), Plate VI, via Project Gutenberg #65918
caption: A black-and-white photograph of the same scene. In this view the stitched comet, with its fiery tail, is easy to see on the original cloth.

title: Halley's Comet, 1066 (from the Bayeux Tapestry)
creator: Unknown draughtsman (book illustration)
why_public_domain: A line copy printed in 1910 in Emerson's book. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Edwin Emerson, Comet Lore: Halley's Comet in History and Astronomy (New York: Schilling, 1910), via Project Gutenberg #66824
caption: A clean outline copy of the comet scene, made for readers in 1910, when the comet came back. It shows the onlookers' pointing hands and the star with its streaming tail.

title: Edmund Halley
creator: Unknown engraver, after an eighteenth-century portrait
why_public_domain: A portrait engraving printed in 1910. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Edwin Emerson, Comet Lore (New York, 1910), via Project Gutenberg #66824
caption: Edmund Halley printed a map before the eclipse of 3 May 1715 showing where in England the Sun would go dark. He asked people across the country to send in what they saw. His forecast missed by only about four minutes.

title: "Baily's Beads," four stages
creator: After Francis Baily (book illustration)
why_public_domain: A figure in George Chambers's 1899 book. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: George F. Chambers, The Story of Eclipses (London: George Newnes, 1899), Fig. 9, via Project Gutenberg #24222
caption: The last bright points of sunlight breaking up along the Moon's rough edge. The drawing comes from Baily's observation of 1836. In 1715 Halley described something related: a long, narrow streak of dusky red light along the Moon's edge just before and after totality.

title: Rays of light seen near the time of totality
creator: Unknown engraver (book illustration)
why_public_domain: A figure in George Chambers's 1899 book. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: George F. Chambers, The Story of Eclipses (London, 1899), Fig. 7, via Project Gutenberg #24222
caption: A Victorian picture of long rays reaching out around the darkened Sun. It is a general illustration, not a drawing of 1715. Halley and other observers that year described a pale ring of light around the Moon, which we now call the corona.

title: The Falling Stars, Nov. 13, 1833
creator: Adolf Vollmy, wood engraving after a drawing by Karl Jauslin
date: Event 13 November 1833; engraving first published 1889; this printing 1920
why_public_domain: A wood engraving first printed in 1889 and reprinted here in a 1920 US book. Jauslin died in 1904. It is out of copyright in the US and generally treated as public domain everywhere.
original_holder: Bible Readings for the Home Circle (Washington, D.C.: Review & Herald, 1920 edition), p. 323, via Project Gutenberg #34520
caption: The best-known picture of the 1833 storm: meteors streak down over a village street while people stare, pray or point. The artist made it more than fifty years later. The book printed it as a fulfilled sign of the end times, a reading many Americans gave the event then.

title: Falling Stars at Niagara
creator: Unknown engraver (book illustration)
why_public_domain: A book illustration printed in the US in 1920. It is out of copyright in the US. The artist is not named.
original_holder: Bible Readings for the Home Circle (Washington, D.C.: Review & Herald, 1920 edition), p. 319, via Project Gutenberg #34520
caption: Meteors pour down over Niagara Falls. Observers there in 1833 wrote that the sky seemed to rain fire above the roaring water.

title: The meteor storm of 1833 over Niagara (chromolithograph)
creator: After Edmund Weiss, Bilderatlas der Sternenwelt (identification is ours; OpenStax gives no credit)
why_public_domain: A colour print from an 1888 star atlas. It is out of copyright everywhere. OpenStax publishes it without any credit line, so we attribute it to Weiss from the known plate.
original_holder: Edmund Weiss, Bilderatlas der Sternenwelt (Esslingen, 1888); reproduced in OpenStax Astronomy 2e, Fig. 14.1
caption: A colour version of the same scene, drawn more than fifty years after the event and, as OpenStax puts it, "with a bit of artistic license": coloured meteors over the falls. This is a small copy.

title: Shooting Stars of November 12, 1799
creator: Unknown engraver, "from a contemporary drawing"
why_public_domain: A wood engraving in the 1904 English edition of Flammarion's book. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Camille Flammarion, Astronomy for Amateurs (New York: Appleton, 1904), Fig. 55, via Project Gutenberg #25267
caption: The same November meteor stream, seen at sea 34 years earlier. Humboldt watched this 1799 storm from South America. Comparing it with 1833 is how astronomers first realized the storms come back roughly every 33 years.

title: Probable Orbit of the November Meteors
creator: Daniel Kirkwood (diagram)
why_public_domain: A diagram in an 1867 American book. Kirkwood died in 1895. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Daniel Kirkwood, Meteoric Astronomy (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1867), via Project Gutenberg #43715
caption: The answer to the 1833 puzzle: a long loop that carries the meteor swarm out past Uranus and back across Earth's orbit. Denison Olmsted of Yale saw in 1833 that all the meteors came from one point in Leo, and his finding led to this picture.

title: Spots and faculae on the Sun
creator: Warren De la Rue (photograph)
why_public_domain: A photograph taken in 1861. De la Rue died in 1889. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Robert S. Ball, The Story of the Heavens (London, 1897), Plate III, via Project Gutenberg #27378
caption: One of the first good photographs of sunspots, taken two years after the Carrington event. Richard Carrington was sketching a large group of spots like these on 1 September 1859 when two points of white light flared up inside it. It was the first solar flare anyone recorded.

title: Streamers of Aurora Borealis, 28 November 1893
creator: Fridtjof Nansen (pastel sketch)
why_public_domain: A pastel by Nansen, who died in 1930. It was published in 1897 and is out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Fridtjof Nansen, Farthest North, Vol. II (New York: Harper, 1897), Plate XIII, via Project Gutenberg #34120
caption: Northern lights drawn from life aboard the Fram, frozen into the Arctic ice. It is not a picture of 1859. In 1859 lights like these reached as far south as Cuba and Hawaii, and people in the northern United States could read newspapers by them at midnight.

title: Aurora Borealis, 18 October 1894
creator: Fridtjof Nansen (pastel sketch)
why_public_domain: A pastel by Nansen, who died in 1930. It was published in 1897 and is out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Fridtjof Nansen, Farthest North, Vol. II (1897), Plate XV, via Project Gutenberg #34120
caption: Folding curtains of aurora over the pack ice, drawn by an eyewitness. It gives the colours and shapes that people described in 1859. That storm spread such displays across much of the world.

title: An Auroral Crown, December 1894
creator: Fridtjof Nansen (pencil sketch)
why_public_domain: A drawing by Nansen, who died in 1930. It was published in 1897 and is out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Fridtjof Nansen, Farthest North, Vol. II (1897), Plate XVI, via Project Gutenberg #34120
caption: The aurora seen straight overhead, with rays streaming out from a single point. During the 1859 storm, "coronas" like this were reported much farther south than usual.

title: Halley's Comet of 1910, as seen in New York
creator: Unknown illustrator (book frontispiece)
why_public_domain: A frontispiece printed in a US book in 1910. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Edwin Emerson, Comet Lore (New York: Schilling, 1910), frontispiece, via Project Gutenberg #66824
caption: The comet hangs low in the western sky beside the Metropolitan Life tower, then the tallest building in the world. This is an artist's view for readers in May 1910, not a photograph.

title: Halley's Comet, 4 May 1910
creator: E. E. Barnard, Yerkes Observatory (photograph)
why_public_domain: A 1910 photograph by Barnard, who died in 1923. It is out of copyright everywhere. The 1926 book it was copied from is also public domain in the US.
original_holder: Mary Proctor, The Romance of Comets (New York: Harper, 1926), facing p. 110, via Project Gutenberg #75545
caption: Barnard photographed the comet before dawn in Wisconsin on a bitterly cold morning. Its tail stretches across the plate. The short dashes are stars that trailed while the camera followed the comet.

title: Halley's Comet and the planet Venus, 5 May 1910
creator: Union Observatory, Johannesburg (photograph; photographer not named)
why_public_domain: A 1910 observatory photograph. It is out of copyright everywhere. The 1926 book it was copied from is also public domain in the US.
original_holder: Mary Proctor, The Romance of Comets (1926), facing p. 94, via Project Gutenberg #75545
caption: A one-hour exposure from South Africa. The comet's tail streams up toward the top of the frame, and the overexposed disc at lower right is Venus. The comet was well placed for southern observers that spring.

title: Halley's Comet, 6 June 1910
creator: E. E. Barnard, Yerkes Observatory (photograph)
why_public_domain: A 1910 photograph by Barnard, who died in 1923. It is out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Mary Proctor, The Romance of Comets (1926), facing p. 124, via Project Gutenberg #75545
caption: The comet on its way out, a month after Earth passed through its tail on 18–19 May. Many people had feared that night and some bought "comet pills". Nothing happened.

title: The comet of 1910 and the pilgrimage to Talpa
creator: Unknown illustrator (book illustration)
why_public_domain: An illustration printed in a US book in 1910. It is long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Edwin Emerson, Comet Lore (1910), via Project Gutenberg #66824
caption: Pilgrims on mules and on foot head toward a church under the comet. The book quotes the Mexican Herald: the comet "so alarmed the people of Mexico that many thousands went on a holy pilgrimage to the shrine of Talpa in Xalisco."

title: William the Conqueror (An English Dream)
creator: Unknown cartoonist, Kladderadatsch (Berlin)
why_public_domain: An unsigned 1910 magazine cartoon, reprinted in a US book that same year. It is long out of copyright.
original_holder: Kladderadatsch (Berlin), 1910, reprinted in Edwin Emerson, Comet Lore (1910), via Project Gutenberg #66824
caption: A German cartoon from 1910, probably poking fun at British fears of invasion during the naval race: the comet returns, and so, in an "English dream", do Norman invaders landing from the sea. It shows how the 1066 story came back with the comet.

title: Eclipse instruments at Sobral
creator: C. Davidson (photograph), Royal Observatory Greenwich expedition
why_public_domain: A 1919 expedition photograph published in 1920 as the frontispiece of Eddington's book. It is public domain in the US. Davidson was a Royal Observatory staff member, so it was probably Crown copyright, which has long expired (see report).
original_holder: A. S. Eddington, Space, Time and Gravitation (Cambridge, 1920), frontispiece, via Project Gutenberg #29782
caption: The telescopes the British team set up at Sobral in northern Brazil: a coelostat mirror (left) feeding the long camera tubes under a canvas shelter. The 4-inch lens here took the plates that gave the decisive result.

title: Positions of the stars measured in 1919 (Eddington, Fig. 18)
creator: A. S. Eddington (diagram; redrawn for the Project Gutenberg edition)
why_public_domain: A simple diagram from Eddington's 1920 book. Eddington died in 1944. Project Gutenberg's faithful redrawing adds no copyright.
original_holder: A. S. Eddington, Space, Time and Gravitation (1920), Fig. 18, via Project Gutenberg #29782 (vector PDF rendered to PNG)
caption: The stars of the Hyades around the eclipsed Sun. The square marks the plates taken at Príncipe and the tilted rectangle the plates taken at Sobral. Starlight passing near the Sun was found to bend by about the amount Einstein predicted.

title: The eclipse observations (how the Sun bends starlight)
creator: Unknown draughtsman, for E. E. Slosson
why_public_domain: A diagram in a 1920 US popular book. Slosson died in 1929. It is out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Edwin E. Slosson, Easy Lessons in Einstein (New York: Harcourt, Brace and Howe, 1920), via Project Gutenberg #75807
caption: How the public was shown the 1919 result: light from a star is bent as it passes the Sun, so the star seems shifted outward from where it really is. Newspapers around the world reported in November 1919 that Einstein's theory had been confirmed.
